To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
central retinal venal velocity measured by color Doppler imaging is a predictor of conversion from nonis ischemic to ischemic form in patients with retinal vein occlusions.
the risk of ischemic retinal venous occlusion was associated with central retinal venular velocities and retinal hemorrhages.
the risk of ischemic retinal venous occlusion (RVI) is associated with the central retinal venular velocity measured by color Doppler imaging, in a large population of patients with nonischemic RVO.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a study of the relationship between the velocity of blood flow in the central retinal vein and the risk of developing ischemic retinal venous thrombosis (RVO).
the development of new and efficient algorithms for the solution of the nonlinear fractional differential equations.
a study of the conversion from non-ischaemic to ischaemic retinal vein occlusions (RVO).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of CDI for the prediction of the conversion of nonischemia to ischemia in retinal vein occlusions is still in an experimental stage.
the risk of ischemic progression of RVO is associated with central venus velocities and that CDI might be used for identifying risk of conversion.
the risk of ischemic RVO is higher in CRVO and BRVO patients who have an increased CRV, an older age and a high amount of retinal hemorrhages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the risk of ischemic retinopathy is higher in patients with CRVO and BRVO when there is an increase of the central retinal venal velocity after treatment by hemolysis, and that the risk is also high in patients with BRVO when the central retinal vein velocity is elevated on diagnosis.

the risk of ischemic retinopathy in patients suffering from nonischemia RVO is associated with the initial venous velocities measured by color Doppler imaging, with the number of retinal hemorrhages, and with the age of patients.
CDI is a valuable tool to predict conversion from a non-ischemic to an ischemic RVO.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the conversion from nonisemic to ischemic RVO is a real risk for patients with CRVO and BRVO.
central venous velocities, measured by color Doppler imaging, can be used to predict conversion from nonis ischemic to ischemic RVO.
central retinal venular velocities measured by CDI could be used to predict the evolution of RVO.
